articles.title: Grading the 34 Long-Term NHL Contracts Signed During the 2026 Offseason So Far
articles.summary: Every offseason, NHL teams award major contracts hoping those players become long-term building blocks and core roster members. Those deals can come through free agency, following a trade acquisition or by retaining an existing player.
articles.body:
Every offseason, NHL teams award major contracts hoping those players become long-term building blocks and core roster members. Those deals can come through free agency, following a trade acquisition or by retaining an existing player.

In some cases (especially when it comes to free agent investments) those long-term deals can carry significant risks based on the reality you are paying top-dollar on a long-term contract for a player that has likely already played their best hockey for somebody else.

In other cases, the best contract a team signs is the big-money, max-term deal for a player they already have that has not yet reached their prime years.

Given all of that, there have been 34 NHL contracts signed this summer that are five years in length or longer.

We are going to assign a letter grade for all them based on the initial vibes, potential, and long-term risk that come with each one of them. Some teams might end up getting a bargain. Other teams might already be regretting it.

All signings are listed in the order in which they were signed this offseason.

Contract: Six years, $20 million ($3.3 million salary cap)

Michael McCarron is the type of player NHL executives love to obsess over in a way that seems completely disproportionate to the role they play. Depth player, great size and wins face-offs. Teams will crawl over each other to acquire players like this.

For that role, McCarron is a fine player, and the $3.3 million salary cap number isn't anything that's going to break the bank for the Wild.

But signing a 31-year-old version of this player at that number for six years just seems needlessly excessive.

Contract: Eight years $68 million ($8.5 million)

The Maple Leafs needed to address their defense in a major way this offseason, and Raddysh was the top defenseman to enter the market. They acquired him in a sign-and-trade with the Tampa Bay Lightning and made him a key part of their core with an eight-year, $68 million deal.

If Raddysh is able to duplicate his 2025-26 performance, that's a great contract.

The question is whether or not he can do that, and whether or not he can do that for several years.

He did not become an NHL player he was 25 years old. He did not become a full-time player until he was 27 years old. His first two years were good, but not great. His first truly great, breakout year came when he was 29 years old.

They are banking on his most recent performance being a sign of what is to come over the next eight years. As we have seen time and time again in the NHL (and all professional sports) what you did most recently is not necessarily what you will do next. Or consistently.

It could work. He could just be a late-bloomer. But they are taking a big risk in that.

Contract: Five years, $20 million ($4 million salary cap)

The Edmonton Oilers have to do a better job when it comes to preventing goals.

Part of that has to fall on the goalies. Another big part has to fall on the defensemen. But the forwards have to play a role in that as well, and Dickinson is at least a really, really good defensive player down the middle. He's not going to score much, but he can definitely help shut opposing teams down and will be a solid depth presence defensively.

The criticism here is largely due to the five-year term.

Contract: Six years, $34.5 million ($5.75 million salary cap)

Bobby McMann does a lot of things well, and can be a very effective player. He's going to be a menace on the forecheck, bring some speed to the lineup and probably score 20-25 goals.

There's a place for that on a good team.

The problem is Seattle might not be a particularly good team, and he is pretty much a representation of what its roster is already full of: Good, but not great players that are not really difference-makers.

The salary cap hit for what he is in the short-term is pretty much right where it should be. But he is going to be 30 years old when that contract begins. How well is his production and style of play going to hold up into his mid-30s?

Contract: Five years, $20.5 million ($4.1 million salary cap)

Stan Bowman loves his former Chicago Blackhawks, and he apparently sees Murphy as a big part of their defensive turnaround this season.

At his best, Murphy was an outstanding defensive player on some bad Chicago Blackhawks teams where he never had much chance to shine (or find team success). He's a little older now, has maybe lost a step, and probably isn't quite as effective as he was earlier in his career.

Even with that, he should still be one of the better defensive players on the roster, but there is a concern as to how this contract will age and if Edmonton is going to lean on him to do too much or play too big of a role.

Contract: Eight years. $84 million ($10.5 million salary cap)

The Washington Capitals made some big splashes this offseason, and in the process addressed two of their biggest issues from the 2025-26 season: Goal-scoring and generating offense off the rush.

The trade for Jordan Kyrou and acquisition of Alex Tuch should go a long way toward fixing both.

Tuch's contract is the classic case of a deal that's probably going to work out very well in the short-term, but age very poorly by the time it is over.

He has been a pretty consistent 30-goal scorer the past few years, and he might still have a few more years of that level in him before he really starts to slow down. The Capitals should not count on that same level of production from a 34, 35 or 36-year-old Tuch. If they can win big before it gets to that point, with Tuch playing a big role in that, nobody in Washington is going to care.

Contract: Five years, $22.5 million ($4.5 million salary cap)

Kulak was a really strong mid-season addition for the Avalanche, and had some big moments for them in the playoffs. He's also been a really underrated player at times throughout his career. All good signs.

But the downside here is that he is going to be 33 years old this season, and is probably going to start ending up on the downside of his career sooner rather than later, if he already has not.

As a depth player on a contender, he can be a very effective role player. But a five-year term is a little much. He will probably be playing for somebody else before that contract expires.

Contract: Seven years, $52.5 million ($7.5 million salary cap)

Now this is the type of contract that can pay off long-term for a team.

Benson's 2025-26 season (and playoff run) was a little bit of a breakout performance offensively as he scored 13 goals with 43 points in only 65 games. He folloed that up with an outstanding playoff showing as the Sabres reached Game 7 of the second round.

The important thing to remember with all of that: He is still only 20 years old. His best days are still coming.

He might not ever be a big-time scorer or the player you build the team around, but he will score enough to be effective while also being one of the NHL's best pests for the next decade.

Contract: Five years, $37 million ($7.4 million salary cap)

Ken Holland has made some curious and regrettable deals with his defense since taking over the Los Angeles Kings (signing Cody Ceci and Brian Dumoulin to long-term contracts; trading Jordan Spence), but the Clarke contract is not one of them.

He is already a good player, is still only 23 years old, and is now signed throughout his prime years at what should be a below market rate for a top-pairing defender (which Clarke already is).

Compared to some other contracts signed by similar age defensemen this summer, including several that are not as good as Clarke, this is a big win for Holland and the Kings.

Contract: Seven years, $77 million ($11 million salary cap)

You have to give the New York Rangers some credit here for making a sizable investment (both in terms of trade assets and money) into a player that is actually in the prime of his career, and is not some former big-name that is simply trying to drag their decaying bag of bones across the finish line of their career.

This is a new twist for the Rangers, and when you combine it with adding some defensemen that can actually skate and move the puck a little bit they have had a sneaky good offseason.

Is Dorofeyev the type of player you are going to build the whole team around and make the focal point of your roster? No. But is he a player you want on your team that can make a big impact for you? Heck yes. He is going to score a lot of goals, and that is important. Good player. Good move. Good contract.

New general manager Chris MacFarland brought a lot of his former players with him from Colorado, and Drury was one of them. He gave him a nice raise at five years and $22.5 million, which is a little steep for a player that's right on the line between the third-and fourth-line. Even if he is good at that role.

The one nice thing he has going for him is that he still only 27 years old, so there's not a huge risk that he is going to totally fall off anytime soon.

If anything, this is a good reminder as to how much salaries are rising with the salary cap going up.

Contract: Six years, $75 million ($12.5 million salary cap)

Bowen Byram's deal with the Chicago Blackhawks is going to be hockey's version of a Rorschach test for the next six years.

Everybody is going to see something different.

Some people are going to look at this and see a defenseman that plays a lot of minutes, on a bad team, and puts up 55-60 points and say that he is worth the cost and worth the trade (picks No. 4 and 45 and defenseman Louis Crevier) to acquire him.

Others are going to look at this and see a flawed defensive player that does not really drive possession or control the game and wonder why he is being paid like a No. 1 defenseman when he does not actually play like a No. 1 defenseman.

There was nothing wrong with Chicago trading the No. 4 overall pick (or the No. 45 overall pick) for somebody that can help them right now. They need to get better, and they need to get better quickly. It is tough to question that mindset.

It is a little easier to question if they spent all of that on the right player.

Byram will not be a bad player or a liability. He should improve them. He just might not be what they are paying him to be, or improve them as much as the current management thinks he will.

Contract: six years, $17.5 million ($2.91 million salary cap)

Beck Malenstyn's contract with the Sabres is very similar to the McCarron deal with the Wild. The cap hit is fine. It's not something you're going to lose sleep over and he can be an effective depth player. But why do you need to sign a depth player like this for six years? These guys are always available and they are always affordable. There is also not much upside here to be more than what he has already showed himself to be.

It's not a terrible contract, but it's the type of little thing where if you make too many of them they eventually add up into a big problem.

Contract: Six years, $24 million ($4 million salary cap)

Even though their goalies attempted to sabotage it for most of the regular season, the Golden Knights were one of the better defensive teams in the league in 2025-26 and Lauzon played 68 games for that group. He is not going to provide much offensive from a goals and points perspective, and he is probably best suited for a third-pairing role. That makes the six-year contract a little much, especially as he enters his age 29 season. He's a depth player that is going to play most of this contract in his 30s. There is some big risk with all of that.

Contract: Eight years, $40 million ($5 million salary cap)

It is easy for a player like Eetu Luostarinen to get lost on a team like Florida where there are All-Stars and big-name players all over the roster. But he is a perfect fit for the role they need him to play and a really, really good two-way player. He defends extremely well and scores enough to be an effective two-way complementary piece on a contending team.

He is also at an age (28) where the contract should age fairly well into his 30s.

The $5 million cap hit is also only going to look better as the cap continues to rise.

Contract: Five years, $58.5 million ($11.7 million salary cap)

In terms of value against the salary cap, overall production, age of the player and quality of the player this is one of the best signings and contracts of the summer.

Hischier is a legit top-line center that plays a complete two-way game, and along with Jack Hughes gives the Devils one of the best center duos in the league.

Is the team around them good enough to compete? Not yet. But they have two really important pieces in place, and between the two of them they are signed for less than $20 million over the next few years.

Contract: Seven years, $59.5 million ($8.5 million salary cap)

The Vegas Golden Knights roster construction always seems to follow the same three-point play.

Re-sign big-name player to huge contract

Ask questions and figure everything else out later

Vegas has played in three Stanley Cup Finals in its first nine years in the league and is a serious contender every year. They are doing something right.

Sometimes, however, even the best and most successful teams can get themselves in trouble and fly a little too close to the sun and get burned in the process.

I fear this is what is going to happen with Andersson on this contract. I'm not sure how good he is still is right now (despite the big offensive numbers this past season), or how well he is going to age now that he is into his 30s.

Contract: Six years, $9 million ($1.5 million)

Acquiring Brady Tkachuk and Radko Gudas in the same offseason, and putting them on a team with Matthew Tkachuk, Brad Marchand and Sam Bennett, is one of the most diabolical roster constructions in the league. Every game is going to turn into a circus. And maybe that is what Florida wants?

The cap hit here is negligible, but there is something weird about signing a 36-year-old player to a six-year contract.

Florida isn't going to be asking Gudas to play a major role, but even in limited action there is some question as to how good he can still be. There might even be a risk he does something reckless in a big moment to cost them. Then again, you could probably say that about half of the roster.

Contract: Eight years, $73.2 million ($9.15 million salary cap)

The Canadiens have put together one of the best young cores in the league and have managed to get all of them signed to long-term deals that should age tremendously over the years. Demidov's eight-year deal this offseason is the most recent of those contracts.

While he has only played one full season in the league, he has shown every sign of being an All-Star level scorer and dynamic playmaker for the next decade (or more).

In most normal years his 19-goal, 63-point season at age 20 would have made him a near Calder Trophy lock. But because he was playing in the league at the same time as Matthew Schaefer he had to settle for second place.

Assuming he continues to progress, his $9.15 million salary cap hit through his prime years in the NHL is going to look like a steal as the cap continues to climb.

Contract: Five years, $27.5 million ($5.5 million salary cap)

Vladar was awesome for the Flyers in 2025-26. He was probably more than awesome. He was not only one of the better free agent signings in the 2025 class, he was one of the biggest difference-makers in getting the Flyers in the playoffs and through to the second round.

That earned him a new long-term contract with the Flyers.

Here's the problem and why I don't love it -- at no point in his career has he ever shown an ability to play at that level consistently. In fact, prior to the 2025-26 season he was consistently one of the least productive and least effective goalies in the NHL.

Goalies are weird. Sometimes everything clicks at a random point in their career and they go on a completely different path and figure it all out.

The counter to that is sometimes bad goalies just have a random great year and never repeat it.

Contract: Eight years, $56.8 million ($7.1 million salary cap)

This might be one of the more underrated long-term contracts of the offseason.

Foerster does not get as much attention as some of the other young players in the Flyers' rebuild (Matvei Michkov, Porter Martone), but he has quickly become one of their most important and effective players for both now and the future.

He is still only 24 years old, is already a tremendous defensive player in some of the toughest minutes on the team, and has proven himself capable of scoring more than 20 goals over a full season. His 13 goals in 29 games in 2025-26 had him on track to blow past that number.

That level of offense, combined with his defense, makes him one of the game's better young two-way wingers, and the Flyers have him locked through all of his prime years at a very affordable rate.

Contract: Five years, $12.5 million ($2.5 million salary cap)

This feels like a direct response (and maybe overreaction) to the Florida Panthers bulking up their legion of goons (said with love). And if you want to respond to that as a divisional rival, fair enough. More power to you. But five years? Excessive.

Contract: Five years, $33.75 million ($6.75 million salary cap)

Marchment's deal with the Sharks was one of the bigger free agent contracts, and while it is a little pricey, it's exactly what the Sharks needed.

So much of San Jose's 2025-26 season was dependent on Macklin Celebrini carrying the team. They were absolutely dominated during 5-on-5 play when he was not on the ice, and building up the depth (at both forward and defense) had to be a priority this offseason.

They addressed the defense with the Darnell Nurse trade and Jacob Trouba signing.

The addressed the forward situation with the Marchment signing.

He's an outstanding two-way veteran that can defense and chip in legitimate second-line offense. It might not age well by year five, but it will be a big upgrade the next couple of seasons.

Shea is coming off a really good (and surprising) season for the Pittsburgh Penguins, and the Oilers are hoping some of that solid play can transfer out west.

If they are counting on him to be a third-line defender, and maybe occasionally slide up into the second-pairing, they should be happy with what they get. It's a little long on the term for a depth player, but the price is fair.

It's not an exciting move by any means, but it should help.

Contract: Five years, $90 million ($18 million salary cap)

The Philadelphia Flyers shocked the hockey world by signing Carlsson to a five-year offer sheet in restricted free agency, making him at the time the highest-paid player in the league.

The Ducks eventually matched it, and they pretty much had to given Carlsson's importance.

Bottom line -- this is an overpay, and probably not a small one. That is the only thing that keeps it from being an A. Carlsson is still really good. Outstanding, even. He is on his way to being a No. 1 center and is Anaheim's franchise cornerstone. But he's not an $18 million player in this market. Not now. Probably not ever. Almost certainly not within the next five years.

But it doesn't mean it's a bad contract for the Ducks. They are still going to get value out of it, and if you are going to overpay somebody, the top-line stars are the easiest to make it work.

Contract: Six years, $33 million ($5.5 million salary cap)

Under the leadership of McFarland in his first year running the team, the Nashville Predators decided not to begin a rebuild and shed veteran players, but to instead keep trying to win with the core they had and complement it with a number of depth players.

Mavrik Bourque is one of the more intriguing additions because he still has some untapped upside that could see him reach a higher level of production.

Bourque has played just two full seasons in the NHL, and saw his production take a big jump from year one to year two, going from 11 goals and 25 assists as a rookie, to 20 goals and 41 points this past season.

Even if Bourque stays at that level of play, a 25-year-old forward that can score 20 goals is well worth a $5.5 million salary cap hit through their mid-late 20s. If he progresses beyond that, it's a steal.

Contract: Five years, $36 million ($7.2 million salary cap)

This felt like a bit of a panic move given the threat of a potential offer sheet, which Anaheim already had to deal with in the Carlsson situation. It's also probably a little more than they wanted (or intended) to pay him this summer.

Mintyukov has played three full seasons in the NHL and flashed top-four potential at times, but his game is still a very unfinished product.

He's being paid like a top-pairing defenseman but has not consistently been there yet. That doesn't mean he won't get there.

Given his contract, as well as the departures Anaheim has had on its blue line this offseason, he is going to need to have a big breakout season to keep Anaheim from regressing in the standings.

Contract: Five years, $36.25 million ($7.25 million)

The Flames are deep into a rebuild and had a surplus of first-round picks over several years and decided to cash two of them in to acquire Nemec from the New Jersey Devils, and then sign him to a five-year deal.

It's an intriguing move because Nemec definitely fits in with the right age group the Flames should be looking for, and there is some potential here offensively. The key to this contract being a win, and the Flames improving as a team, is going to be Nemec rounding out the rest of his game to become a more impactful player in ways beyond just producing points.

Contract: Five years, $30 million ($6 million salary cap)

Winnipeg is going to need a lot of things to go right this season to bounce back from a dreadful 2025-26 season, and a big breakout season from Perfetti has to be high on the list.

He's been a pretty consistent scorer in terms of what his production looks like (about 17 goals and 40 total points over 82 games), but the Jets probably want to see a little more.

For $6 million per season over five years they are going to need a little bit more.

At the moment it's maybe a small overpay, but nothing outrageous. A little improvement and a little more offense could make it a slightly below market deal.

Contract: Six years, $40.5 million ($6.7 million salary cap)

The Blues are taking some big gambles this offseason, and McMichael is one of them.

He was one of the key pieces in the trade that sent Jordan Kyrou to the Washington Capitals.

He's a perfectly fine player right now. A good, middle-six player that can score and is still in his mid-20s. The question that has to be answered is whether or not he can take another step forward and go from a 15-20 goal scorer, to a more consistent 25-30 scorer.

Even if he doesn't, a $6.7 million cap hit is not a terrible overpay for what he is. But the Blues really need players like him and Mason McTavish to work out for their plan to work.

Contract: Five years, $75 million ($15 million salary cap)

Given the contracts for some of the other top young players in the league this offseason, getting Bedard at $15 million is probably just about right. The only potential flaws are that for as good as Bedard is offensively, he is still a very unfinished product defensively and has already started to build up a concerning run of injuries early in his career.

The five-year term also continues a trend of young players signing shorter term deals, going right into unrestricted free agency.

Given how bad the Blackhawks been early on on Bedard's career, there has to be some pressure to show him they can build a contender around him. So far, they have failed.

Contract: Eight years, $54 million ($6.75 million salary cap)

John Marino is not the flashiest defenseman in the league, and he is not going to put up the biggest numbers, nor is he going to play an overly physical game. But he is simply a rock-solid, steady defensive player that has found a home in Utah.

Is there some risk with an eight-year contract for a 29-year-old defenseman? Sure there is. But a $6.75 million salary cap number for a legitimate top-four defenseman is going to be a really strong deal in the coming years.

Marino and Nate Schmidt also helped form one of the NHL's most effective (and underrated) defensive duos in the league this past season.

Contract: Five years, $94 million ($18 million salary cap)

Some contracts you simply do not need to overthink.

Celebrini is not only the best young player in the league, he is one of the best players in the league regardless of age.

He is also still just entering his age 20 season and is likely to only get better.

It's a huge win-win contract for both the team and him. From a team perspective, they do not have to deal with him as a restricted free agent next summer. From his perspective, he gets to be one of the highest-paid players in the league and still set himself up for another massive payday when he is still in his mid-20s.

Contract: Eight years, $32 million ($4 million salary cap)

The most shocking long-term contract of the offseason was the Pittsburgh Penguins decision to sign forward Ville Koivunen to an eight-year contract worth $32 million after just 50 NHL games and only two goals.

But the Penguins view it as a low-risk with a potentially high reward.

If Koivunen can turn into an effective second-or third-line scorer (which he absolutely has the talent to do) it's going to be a very cap-friendly deal.

If he doesn't, because of his age they can buy him out within two years and only be on the hook for a salary cap hit of $750,000 each year as a part of it.

Koivunen's underlying numbers were some of the best on the Penguins this past season, but he needs to turn it into more tangible production and offense.

articles.title: Pro wrestling star Austin Aries shares thoughts on celebrities entering the sport
articles.summary: MLW openweight champion Austin Aries calls celebrity involvement in pro wrestling potentially insulting to those who put in years of hard work.
articles.body: Celebrities and professional athletes from outside the ring have been a part of the pro wrestling world for quite some time. The first WrestleMania featured Mr. T, Cyndi Lauper, Muhammad Ali, Billy Martin and Liberace and the tradition of using actors, actresses, musical artists and traditional professional athletes has continued for the last four decades. WWE, for instance, has used Jelly Roll, Lil Yachty and others recently for roles even outside the WrestleMania spectacle. COMPLETE PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE ON OUTKICK Major League Wrestling (MLW) openweight champion Austin Aries admitted he’s more of a "traditionalist" when it comes to professional wrestling. He told OutKick in a recent interview he understands the entertainment aspect of his sport, but shudders at the possibility of those outside the ring taking away opportunities from those putting in the work. "I think balance is key, right? I'm probably more of a traditionalist in a lot of sense, but I also understand at the end of the day this is entertainment," Aries said. "And so, even going back to, the first WrestleMania, I mean, it was about bringing in celebrities. I grew up more of a rasslin’ fan as opposed to a sports entertainment fan. So, I'll always kind of skew towards being more traditional. ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW! "And also, I think the important part is, for a lot of us who have, like, this has been our career, we've had to work very hard for a very long time to perfect what we do. And to take someone because they're a celebrity and roll out a red carpet and let them take shortcuts and let them do things in a way that kind of skirts all that hard work that a lot of us men and women have put in, frankly, it can be insulting. It can be disrespectful at points. I understand about wanting to sell more tickets and get more eyes on the product, but you can't do that at the expense of the people that are in there week in and week out putting the work in." Aries spoke to OutKick before his three-way match against Místico and Averno aired on MLW’s "Fusion" last weekend. He put the MLW Openweight Championship on the line against both men and walked out the winner. He also took Místico’s mask as a souvenir. articles.title: NHL Sets Sights On TV Market Expansion Ahead Of New Rights Deal
articles.summary: The NHL is aiming to choose between Houston and Austin for its 33rd franchise by year's end, and also has major TV markets like Atlanta and Phoenix in mind f...
articles.body:
The NHL is planning to expand yet again, and could award a 33rd franchise to either Austin or Houston by the end of the year.

The Athletic 's Chris Johnston reported the news after speaking with league deputy commissioner Bill Daly. It's a natural next step after the NHL secured an agreement from Daniel Friedkin's Pursuit Sports group in July to pay a $2 billion expansion fee for an Austin or Houston franchise.

While the fee is about three times what the Seattle Kraken paid ($650 million) when that franchise entered the league for the 2021-22 season, franchise values have also ballooned significantly in the time since.

Forbes ' own NHL team valuation list from 2025 shows over half of the league's franchises are worth at least $2 billion. The Toronto Maple Leafs lead the way there at $4.4 billion, with the New York Rangers at $4 billion. In Dallas , the expansion team's would-be rival the Stars is estimated to be worth $2.3 billion.

So if anything, one could argue that $2 billion for a team set to play in Houston or Austin could be a steal of a price. Especially in Houston, where there's a significant billionaire class ready to throw capital at a hockey franchise, and the No. 6 U.S. media market to draw additional interest.

That media market sits at the center of this expansion idea for the NHL, which has been more aggressive in terms of adding teams this century than its peers in the NBA, NFL and MLB.

Hockey has added four franchises (Columbus, Minnesota, Las Vegas and Seattle) to its ranks since 2000, along with club relocations to Winnipeg and Salt Lake City. During the same stretch, the NFL and NBA added one team apiece, while MLB has stood pat.

A 33-team NHL would be North America's largest major sports league. And that's before the eventual expansion to 34. Daly's comments to The Athletic also make it clear those conversations are ongoing – again, with some of the largest available media markets.

Increasingly Murky Media Landscape For Hockey

Hockey purists would likely prefer that if the NHL is going to return to an abandoned market, Quebec City would be first on the list.

Yet, given the success of the league's southern expansion in recent decades, it's hard to argue against continuing the strategy. Especially when there are still major U.S. TV markets without teams and the NHL is about to start negotiations for a new rights deal following the 2027-28 season.

The current 32-team membership makes about $625 million per year from Disney and Warner Bros. Discovery in the U.S. Estimates on the next media deal vary, but given traditional media cuts, increased TV rights across the board and larger industry consolidation, it's still unknown just how much this next NHL contract could net from broadcast and cable partners.

Pulling in streaming-exclusive partners could mean more media revenues, but also reduced attention (as MLS and Formula 1 are contending with on Apple TV to varying extents).

Since the powers-that-be in the NHL certainly know this and only have so much control over resources available to broadcast hockey games, they're pulling the only lever they have for immediate, guaranteed revenue growth: Expansion.

Specifically, expansion in top media markets that currently lack a team.

Fortunately or unfortunately for the NHL, that means not treading new ground in untapped markets, but revisiting cities where it didn't work out previously – sometimes multiple times.

Daly noted Phoenix and Atlanta, respectively No. 7 and No. 12 among U.S. TV markets, as the two cities in ongoing discussions for team No. 34.

The Phoenix area was home to the Coyotes from 1996 to 2024 after the team relocated from Winnipeg. But the team long struggled with financial and arena issues, and even played its final two seasons at Arizona State's Mullett Arena (seating capacity of 4,600). The team's assets were eventually moved to Utah to comprise the "expansion" Mammoth . But the Coyotes' history and marks remain in Arizona.

Atlanta, meanwhile, has been home to two separate franchises in the past.

The Atlanta Flames played in Downtown Atlanta from 1972 to 1980, before they relocated to Calgary . The city got a second NHL try in 1999 with the expansion Atlanta Thrashers, who also played downtown (splitting Philips Arena with the NBA's Hawks). However, that team would also find itself in Canada, when the Thrashers were purchased and moved to Winnipeg – to become the new Jets – in 2011.

Past failures in these markets don't necessarily indicate future issues. Hockey infrastructure in both metropolitan areas could be significantly improved, and arena locations (for Atlanta, nearby Alpharetta has approved an arena for a potential NHL team) could make a major difference as well.

But by the same token, some of the factors that made those cities difficult business propositions previously could also be the case once again. Regardless of how large those media markets may be.

The NHL, as a whole, could potentially see the benefit of adding major markets and expansion fees in the $2 billion range as outweighing the impact on competitiveness and overall roster talent. However, if adding teams that underperform makes the on-ice product worse as a result, it could potentially hurt the league's TV negotiations next time around.

Of course, there's also the potential that it doesn't.

In college sports, the Big Ten's additions of market-based schools outside of its footprint (particularly Rutgers, Maryland and UCLA) hasn't hampered the conference's ability to collect soaring media revenues or win on the field. Still, that's a collection of just 18 colleges, with an automatic mechanism of adding new fans every fall, via student enrollment.

The NHL doesn't have that, but also has more games to leverage for revenue. And as it explores expansion with TV markets as the primary lens, it also has to hope the games it's acquiring deliver both for at-home and in-arena audiences. Because if not, it's unlikely to get another try at adding teams in major (but non-traditional for hockey) U.S. media hubs.

articles.summary: Esports News: After years of anticipation since it was first revealed, Ananta has officially received a release date, a brand-new gameplay trailer, and a wealth of .
articles.body: After years of anticipation since it was first revealed, Ananta has officially received a release date, a brand-new gameplay trailer, and a wealth of new details about its open world and story. NetEase Games and Naked Rain are finally ready to show the world what they have been building.This is one of the most eagerly awaited free-to-play games in recent memory, with fans extremely excited about its arrival. In the section below, we provide you with everything we know so far about Ananta, including its release date, platforms, gameplay, story, and monetisation model.Ananta release dateNetEase Games and Naked Rain have finally announced the release date for Ananta, and the game is now set to release worldwide on January 15, 2027. articles.title: Israel-Hamas truce failure ‘point of no return,’ envoy warns
articles.summary: Hamas has pledged to hand over its weapons as part of the US plan for Gaza, which Israeli PM Netanyahu has rejected.
articles.body:
The failure of the Gaza ceasefire process would be a “point of no return”, the lead official for the enclave on United States President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace has warned.

Nickolay Mladenov, the board’s high representative for Gaza, made the remark on Wednesday in a statement to the United Nations Security Council.

The assertion followed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s public rejection of Trump’s 15-point peace plan that Washington says is aimed at ending Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

A resumption of fighting in Gaza would mean there would be “no roadmap to return to, there will be no administration to deploy and there will be nothing left on the ground to rebuild. That would not be a setback. It would be a point of no return for everyone,” Mladenov told the council.

Gaza’s Ministry of Health said at least 1,288 Palestinians have been killed and 4,290 wounded since a US-brokered “ceasefire” came into effect in October .

At least 73,422 Palestinians have been killed since attacks by Hamas and other Palestinian groups in southern Israel resulted in about 1,200 people killed and 240 taken captive on October 7, 2023. That same day, Israel began its war on Gaza.

Hamas agreed on July 30 to the US roadmap aimed at moving the ceasefire plan forward. Under it, the decommissioning of weapons would be supervised by an International Stabilization Force, a nascent unit led by US Major General Jasper Jeffers that will be deployed to Gaza if the situation calms.

Hamas has pledged to hand over its weapons to a new Palestinian governing body, a framework that Netanyahu immediately opposed even as Trump hailed the plan as a breakthrough. This month, Netanyahu said Israel would not ⁠⁠withdraw any of its forces until Hamas ⁠⁠fully disarms.

The emerging National Committee for the Administration of Gaza would be made up of independent Palestinian technocrats with the responsibility of managing day-to-day civil service and humanitarian relief.

“For the first time, Hamas and the armed factions in Gaza have agreed to hand over their weapons and to transfer full governing authority – both civilian and security – to a transitional administration recognised by the United Nations,” Mladenov told the UN.

He added that “the second risk [to the ceasefire] runs in the opposite direction. Hamas has committed to cease all military activities. That commitment is still to be met in full.”

Mladenov emphasised that “every weapon carried, every tunnel still worked on and every convoy still obstructed sets the process back and hands an argument to those who want to resume war.”

Meanwhile, Riyad Mansour, the Palestinian ambassador to the UN, told the Security Council that Israeli annexations of Palestinian land are killing prospects for regional peace.

Noting the recent release of bidding tenders for the E1 settlement project in the occupied West Bank, he accused the Israeli government of intentionally undermining the 15-point peace plan.

articles.title: Yankees lose another player to IL, make several roster moves
articles.summary: The Yankees have lost another key piece on their roster.
articles.body:
The New York Yankees have suffered another MLB pitching setback, placing right-hander Fernando Cruz on the 15-day injured list with right elbow discomfort.

The move comes at a particularly difficult time for New York , which is already dealing with multiple injuries on its pitching staff and now has to make several corresponding roster moves .

Oct 4, 2025; Toronto, Ontario, CAN; New York Yankees manager Aaron Boone (17) hands the ball to pitcher Fernando Cruz (63) in the seventh inning against the Toronto Blue Jays during game one of the ALDS round for the 2025 MLB playoffs at Rogers Centre. Mandatory Credit: Dan Hamilton-Imagn Images

Cruz has been an important part of the Yankees' bullpen this season, making his absence another concern for Aaron Boone and the pitching staff. The Yankees announced that Cruz will spend at least the next 15 days on the IL because of the elbow issue.

The move is especially notable because Cruz has been one of New York's most effective strikeout relievers. The right-hander has consistently generated swings and misses and has been relied upon in high-leverage situations.

Now, the Yankees will have to find a way to replace those innings while Cruz recovers.

New York has already placed Max Fried and Ryan Weathers on the injured list this month, leaving the club with less pitching depth than it had entering the stretch run.

Apr 28, 2026; Arlington, Texas, USA; New York Yankees relief pitcher Fernando Cruz (63) reacts after the eighth inning against the Texas Rangers at Globe Life Field. Mandatory Credit: Kevin Jairaj-Imagn Images

The Yankees made several moves alongside Cruz's IL placement.

New York optioned right-hander Bradley Hanner to Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre and recalled right-hander Elmer Rodríguez from Triple-A. Rodríguez is scheduled to start Wednesday against the Houston Astros , giving the Yankees another arm to help navigate the rotation crunch.

The Yankees also signed right-hander Michael Fulmer to a Major League contract and selected him to the active roster. The veteran adds another experienced arm to a bullpen that suddenly needs reinforcements.

Finally, New York transferred right-hander Kervin Castro to the 60-day injured list, creating additional roster flexibility while Castro continues dealing with his right elbow issue.

That's a lot of movement for one day, and it illustrates just how much pressure the Yankees' pitching staff is under.

With the postseason race tightening and several important pitchers unavailable, New York is going to need its reinforcements to contribute immediately.

Losing Cruz is another significant blow, and the Yankees are now relying on a combination of young pitchers and veterans such as Fulmer to keep the bullpen and rotation afloat.

articles.body: A video claiming to show alleged GTA 6 leaker CyberLeek outside a Nuremberg courthouse has taken over social media. This has resulted in a lot of commotion within the gaming community about whether the person behind the leaks has been finally caught.The clip has racked up millions of views in a matter of hours, and is making rounds across different platforms. However, before you take it at face value, there are some very important things to consider.In the section below, we take a look at whether the GTA 6 leaker CyberLeek was outside the Nuremberg courthouse.What does the viral GTA 6 leaker CyberLeek footage show?Phone footage reportedly filmed in Nuremberg, Germany on August 27, 2026 has been viral on social media platforms. It allegedly shows CyberLeek, the individual behind the recently circulated GTA 6 leaks, standing outside a courthouse.In the clip, there was a large crowd of mostly young supporters around the entrance, repeatedly shouting CyberLeek's name. The atmosphere feels far more like a fan meet-and-greet than a court appearance, with phones held aloft from every direction.Before leaving, the individual in the footage pauses for a few moments and signs several final autographs for people at the front of the crowd. Some supporters can be heard cheering while others continue calling for his release as police begin clearing a path.The footage spread rapidly online because of the surreal contrast between an impending detention and the celebrity-like reception outside the courthouse.Is the footage showing GTA 6 leaker CyberLeek real?This is where things get considerably confusing. While the clip has been shared widely and presented as authentic, there are significant reasons to doubt whether the person shown is actually CyberLeek at all.CyberLeek has operated entirely anonymously throughout the GTA 6 leak saga. No verified photographs, videos, or identifying details about the individual behind the alias have ever been made public. That makes it virtually impossible to confirm whether the person in the Nuremberg footage is genuinely CyberLeek or simply someone capitalising on the moment for clout.The timing of the clip, arriving almost simultaneously with Rockstar's campaign against the leaks, has only added to suspicions that the footage may have been staged or misattributed entirely.It is highly likely that the person in the viral footage is not CyberLeek. articles.title: The men who posted themselves between Channel Islands
articles.summary: Harry Turner and Major Palmer's use of little-known postal regulations are being marked by stamps.
articles.body:
One man wanted to test an unusual postal loophole after reading about it in a newspaper while another was desperate to get home to his family as war spread across Europe.

More than 30 years apart, Harry Turner and Major "Peabod" Palmer both travelled between Channel Islands by post.

In 1905, Guernsey resident Turner decided to find out whether the postal system could really be used to transport a person - it had previously been done by a man in London in 1900 .

After reading a newspaper article about the rules, he arranged to be sent from Guernsey to Sark as a postal item, becoming what is believed to have been the first person ever to post himself.

"A bit of a mischievous man," was how Guernsey Post's head of philatelic Bridget Yabsley described Turner.

She said: "I think he decided to say, 'Right, I'm going to test this out,' and he did, and he got himself posted to Sark."

It was a very different set of circumstances for Major Palmer - in February 1940 he was trying to get from Guernsey to Alderney to reunite with his family as war spread across Europe.

All the passenger places on the ferry were booked, but after studying postal regulations, he concluded there was nothing preventing him from travelling under postal supervision.

The ferry captain initially refused to take him because passenger numbers were restricted and he was neither cargo nor mail, but circumstances changed when some booked travellers failed to arrive - although he had to travel in the hold.

Yabsley said when Palmer reached Alderney he was taken to the postal sorting office and was "actually physically handed over to his wife" by a local postman.

Yabsley said she had discovered newspaper articles about the events among Guernsey Post's historic records and thought they would make "quite a nice kind of light-hearted story to tell".

She added: "Harry Turner was the first individual ever to be posted [in the islands], and then Major Palmer was the last.

"So even though they're years apart, we thought it was a really good kind of first and last story that we could tell."

The regulations were later changed, closing the loophole and bringing the era of human parcels to an end.

articles.title: Cross denies history making Beau Greaves in dramatic Budapest encounter
articles.summary: The 2026 European Tour season resumed with a bumper day of action at the MVM Dome, as Cross denied Greaves a dream debut in the Hungarian capital...
articles.body:
Rob Cross overcame Beau Greaves in an incredible opening round tie at the Hungarian Darts Trophy, as reigning champion Niko Springer enjoyed a winning return in Budapest.

The 2026 European Tour season resumed with a bumper day of action at the MVM Dome, as Cross denied Greaves a dream debut in the Hungarian capital.

The three-time Women's World Matchplay champion — the first woman to compete in a European Tour event — averaged 104.88 and posted five 180s in a superb all-round display, only to succumb in a dramatic decider.

"Beau is brilliant. She is going places," insisted Cross, who averaged 101.90 and produced a sensational 170 checkout en route to setting up a clash against Luke Woodhouse.

"She has been phenomenal on the ProTour, and I think when she learns her trade on the big stage, she's going to do more.

"I feel really happy with my set-up at the minute. I think I can do great things, but it's down to me to prove it."

Springer also impressed on Friday's opening day, dispatching Maik Kuivenhoven 6-1 to kickstart his challenge for back-to-back titles in Budapest

."I have so many good memories coming back here," revealed Springer, who will face Ryan Searle for a place in the last 16.

"I had a big smile because I was so happy to be here again, and I cannot wait to play tomorrow!"

Former Hungarian Darts Trophy champions Joe Cullen and Dave Chisnall also tasted opening round success, recording 6-3 victories against Adam Leek and Andras Borbely respectively.Cullen averaged almost 98 and pinned 60% of his attempts at double to triumph, while Chisnall converted 101, 120 and 136 checkouts to book a showdown with Wessel Nijman.

Elsewhere, Krzysztof Ratajski began his bid for back-to-back European Tour titles with a 6-5 victory against Callan Rydz, surviving two match darts to progress to a meeting with Scottish icon Gary Anderson.

There was also delight for two Host Nation qualifiers at the MVM Dome, as Laszlo Kadar and Nandor Major celebrated deciding-leg victories on home soil.Kadar performed brilliantly on his European Tour debut, averaging over 93 to claim the scalp of Daryl Gurney and move through to a tie against fourth seed Jonny Clayton on Saturday evening.

Meanwhile, Major will go head-to-head with Dutch number one Gian van Veen in round two, after conjuring a terrific 124 checkout on the bull to stun Niels Zonneveld in a decider.

Kevin Doets was another high-profile casualty on Day One, squandering 31 darts at double during his shock 6-4 defeat against Finland's Jonas Masalin, while Keane Barry averaged almost 101 in dumping out German number one Martin Schindler.

Tom Sykes also averaged 101 in his 6-1 demolition of Cameron Menzies, as World Matchplay semi-finalist Dirk van Duijvenbode eased past Czechia's David Pisek by the same scoreline.

Van Duijvenbode will take on top seed Luke Humphries in a mouth-watering tussle on Saturday evening, while James Hurrell will face Michael van Gerwen after winning through a compelling affair against Damon Heta to register his first victory on the European Tour stage.

Former European Champion Ritchie Edhouse will take on last year's runner-up Danny Noppert in another eye-catching contest, having rattled off six straight legs in his 6-1 thumping of Connor Scutt.

Elsewhere, Andrew Gilding whitewashed newcomer Milan Biro to race through to round two, before Ryan Joyce and William O'Connor completed Saturday's line-up with wins over Cristo Reyes and Samuel Price.

articles.title: What’s behind Netanyahu’s condemnation of this weekend’s settler pogroms?
articles.summary: Israel’s rhetorical outrage masks a calculated, well-funded campaign to permanently erase Palestinian statehood.
articles.body:
A wave of coordinated Israeli settler attacks swept across the occupied West Bank over the weekend, leaving dozens of Palestinians injured and properties torched.

The pogroms have seen little or no response from Israeli police and soldiers.

Dozens of settlers attacked a Palestinian home in the village of Qusra, south of Nablus, with tear gas and stones, injuring seven people. A Palestinian Red Crescent Society ambulance that attempted to reach the besieged families was also attacked.

Simultaneously, Israeli forces fired tear gas during incursions into the Far’a refugee camp, el-Bireh, and al-Mughayyir. Soldiers also attacked journalists in Hebron’s Old City.

A Palestinian family and an American NBC news crew were assaulted in the village of Jalud. In Arrabeh, two Palestinians were also beaten near the Mevo Dotan settlement, in a weekend of violence against locals by Israeli settlers.

The Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs strongly condemned the escalation, particularly the 20-day siege on al-Mughayyir, describing it as a systematic policy of forced displacement and colonial expansion.

Israeli politicians have launched a coordinated campaign to minimise the public relations damage after the pogroms.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu issued a statement strongly condemning the “criminal acts of violence” in Qusra and Jalud, blaming it on a “handful of rioters” who violated the law, interfered with the military, and harmed Israel’s standing in the world.

He publicly stated that he expected law enforcement authorities to “arrest the rioters and bring them to justice”.

However, this public outrage contrasted sharply with the reality on the ground.

Documented footage captured masked settlers storming the villages of Qusra and Jalud in open pickup trucks, according to Israeli media reports. Despite this visual evidence and Netanyahu’s stated demands, the Israeli police’s West Bank district, under the command of Moshe Pinchi, made zero arrests.

President Isaac Herzog echoed the sentiment , calling the events a “red line”.

Former US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee praised Herzog’s statement and claimed that the half-million Israelis living in the West Bank are “most disgusted by a small group of thugs”.

The Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs declared that the violence carried out by “extremists” stands in complete contradiction to the values of Israel.

Opposition leader Yair Lapid described another weekend of violent rampages as a “moral stain” and said the government’s failure to tackle Israeli violence in the West Bank is a “national disgrace”.

Experts told Al Jazeera that this chorus of condemnation from the Israeli establishment represents a calculated political manoeuvre by the government, which is actively engineering the annexation of the West Bank.

Ehab Jabareen, a writer, analyst, and Palestinian citizen of Israel, said that Netanyahu is pursuing a “political surgical isolation process” to shield the broader settlement project from international scrutiny.

“He puts forward a political equation stating that there are 500,000 legitimate settlers, alongside a few dozen deviants or anomalies,” Jabareen said.

“He wants to punish, or give the illusion of punishing, the most blatant link in order to protect the wider system.”

By defining the latest pogroms as a criminal anomaly, Netanyahu aims to isolate this from the wider settler enterprise, Jabareen added.

Few see the prime minister’s statement as anything more than a practical response to fears among the military that unchecked settler pogroms could ignite a massive Palestinian uprising in the occupied West Bank.

Recent closed-door security assessments by Major General Avi Bluth, head of the Israeli military’s Central Command, warned that “nationalistic crime”, such as the pogroms, could spark a massive response from Palestinians.

“The army speaks to Netanyahu in the language of cost-benefit analysis,” Jabareen noted.

“Dozens of settlers create an open front that requires the mobilisation of thousands of soldiers. Netanyahu did not say this is unacceptable because it targets Palestinians, but rather said it obstructs the army.”

Mamoun Abu Amer, an analyst on Israeli politics, dismissed the idea that the state has lost control over the settlers.

He emphasised that the military consistently protects the settlers during these attacks while heavily punishing Palestinians who attempt to defend themselves.

“The settlers are too cowardly to carry out any attack without the sponsorship and cover of the government,” Abu Amer said, pointing to instances where the military demolished Palestinian homes simply because the residents resisted settler assaults.

While top Israeli officials publicly distance themselves from individual attacks, the government is still systematically funding, legalising, and expanding the settlers’ presence.

A report by the Israeli organisation Peace Now detailed how successive governments, heavily influenced by Netanyahu, have thrived on expanding settlements since the 1993 Oslo Accords.

Thirty years ago, there were approximately 110,000 settlers in the West Bank and 140,000 in East Jerusalem.

Today, those numbers have skyrocketed to 465,000 in the West Bank and 230,000 in East Jerusalem.

The current far-right Israeli government has accelerated this process to unprecedented levels.

According to a 2025 European Union report , the Israeli government officially approved the establishment of 54 new settlements in the West Bank in a single year, a more than tenfold increase from the five approved in 2024.

In parallel, 86 new outposts were erected, and a record-breaking 63,311 units were also approved across the occupied territories.

Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who holds sweeping administrative powers over the territory, recently declared a “ revolution in settlement ” expansion, openly linking the construction to the prevention of Palestinian statehood.

The government recently passed a record $271bn national budget that bypassed legal frameworks to allocate 400 million shekels ($134m) to the Ministry of Settlement and National Missions, which officially authorises illegal outposts.

This massive infrastructure investment includes advancing the strategic E1 settlement project, which could sever the West Bank in two and effectively kill any hope for the establishment of a Palestinian state.

The government recently issued tenders for 1,234 homes as part of a larger plan to build 3,401 units connecting the Ma’ale Adumim settlement to occupied East Jerusalem, as part of this plan.

The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported that settler violence is on the rise, recording over 1,540 attacks that caused Palestinian casualties or property damage this year alone.

OCHA noted that the monthly average of these attacks is now higher than in any other year on record.

Despite this historic surge in state-sponsored pogroms and land theft, Western responses have largely remained confined to rhetorical outrage.

While European nations and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) strongly condemned the recent settlement approvals, including the E1 project, analysts note a glaring double standard.

Abu Amer highlighted that Western countries have failed to impose meaningful economic sanctions on the Israeli state, opting instead to issue travel bans against a few individual settlers.

“There are political positions issued recently by Western countries condemning the Israeli behaviour in reviving the E1 project, but these positions have not translated into practical measures,” Abu Amer said.

He contrasted this hesitation with the immediate actions taken by 28 Western nations to defund the UN agency for Palestinian refugees based on unproven Israeli allegations.

By decoupling the violent acts of individual settlers from the state machinery that arms, funds, and protects them, Israel continues to advance its broader strategic goal: the permanent, irreversible annexation of Palestinian land.

articles.title: ‘National crush’ Major Rishabh Singh Sambyal takes premature retirement after 12 years in Army - His journey from President Murmu’s ADC to internet sensation
articles.summary: For months, Major Rishabh Singh Sambyal was a familiar face beside President Droupadi Murmu at official ceremonies, public engagements and overseas vi.
articles.body: For months, Major Rishabh Singh Sambyal was a familiar face beside President Droupadi Murmu at official ceremonies, public engagements and overseas visits. His military bearing, quiet presence and the occasional glimpse of his work alongside the President turned the otherwise low-profile Army officer into an unlikely social media sensation.Now, the officer who was once widely described online as the internet's “national crush” has moved on from the Indian Army. Sambyal, a former Aide-de-Camp (ADC) to President Murmu, has taken premature retirement after around 12 years of military service.The former ADC met President Murmu after formally leaving his post and expressed gratitude for her guidance and blessings.“Honoured to call on the Hon'ble President of India, Smt. Droupadi Murmu Ji at Rashtrapati Bhavan. The blessings and teachings of the Hon'ble President have helped me grow as an individual in life. Also, it was wonderful to meet the family once again. Jai Hind,” he wrote in an Instagram post, alongside pictures with President Droupadi Murmu.But behind the viral photographs is a military career that began long before Sambyal became recognisable to social-media users.From NDA to the Indian ArmyAccording to Sambyal's publicly available LinkedIn profile, he joined the National Defence Academy after clearing the NDA examination in 2013 and was part of the 133rd NDA course beginning in 2014. His profile also lists his education at the Indian Military Academy, where he studied military studies and defence management.His early military career included an appearance on one of India's most watched ceremonial stages- the Republic Day Parade.In 2021, then-Captain Sambyal led the Jat Regiment contingent at the Republic Day Parade. The contingent went on to win the Best Marching Contingent Trophy, a distinction that brought him professional recognition well before his later association with Rashtrapati Bhavan.He subsequently served with the elite 4 Para Special Forces, popularly associated with the “Daggers”. Reports have also stated that he earned the Balidaan Badge during his Special Forces service.The prestigious President's ADC roleSambyal's career took a particularly high-profile turn when he was selected for the President's ADC assignment.An Aide-de-Camp accompanying the President is far more than a ceremonial figure standing alongside the head of state. The appointment places an officer in close proximity to the President during official engagements and requires attention to protocol, coordination and the demands of a packed schedule.Sambyal's public professional profile describes his experience as involving protocol management, executive security, itinerary coordination and work with senior government officials and foreign dignitaries. It also states that he worked on official diplomatic engagements involving visits to several countries. He was selected as a President's ADC in March 2023, according to the professional information cited in reports about his career.How did Major Sambyal become an internet sensation?The attention around Sambyal was unusual for an Army officer. His appearances alongside President Murmu, particularly during major national events and public engagements, began attracting considerable attention on social media. Users focused on his composed demeanour, formal military appearance and the unobtrusive way he carried out his responsibilities.Earlier in 2026, his photographs from Republic Day-related events again circulated widely. Hindustan Times and Moneycontrol both reported on the attention surrounding the officer, with coverage highlighting how his military bearing and presence had made him a social-media favourite.The nickname “national crush” subsequently became associated with him online. It is worth noting, however, that this is a social-media label, rather than an official designation.Some of the moments that attracted attention were not dramatic military displays at all. Images and videos showing Sambyal carrying out routine duties around the President- including assisting her during public engagements- were widely shared and helped turn an otherwise largely behind-the-scenes appointment into a recognisable public persona.Why did he take premature retirement?There has been no detailed public explanation from the Ministry of Defence setting out the circumstances of his premature retirement. Therefore, claims about a specific reason for his departure should be treated cautiously.An SSB Crack report suggested that he took premature retirement due to personal and family reasons, citing an Instagram Live video. “In everyone’s life there are situations and instances which change your life forever,” he said while revealing that there were no immediate marriage plans.What is clearer is that Sambyal has closed a significant chapter of his military career after about 12 years of service.Sambyal's public professional profile now describes him as a military professional with 12 years of experience in leadership, strategic planning, risk management and operational coordination. What his next move will be remains unclear.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: FIBA Women's World Cup 2026: Team USA hit with major blow involving A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum
articles.summary: International Sports News: Team USA's roster for the FIBA Women's World Cup just took a hit. A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum, two of the most decorated names in USA Basketball, will.
articles.body: Team USA's roster for the FIBA Women's World Cup just took a hit. A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum, two of the most decorated names in USA Basketball, will not suit up in Berlin.USA Basketball confirmed the withdrawals in a Monday statement, and the timing could hardly be worse. With the U.S. chasing a fifth straight World Cup gold and a brutal group stage waiting on the other side, losing this much frontcourt firepower forces a scramble nobody wanted.A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum pull out of USA rosterA'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum are both out of the World Cup for health reasons, USA Basketball announced Monday. Sonia Citron and Kiki Iriafen have already been named as their replacements, and both are in Berlin preparing for the tournament opener against China on Friday.It is a significant loss on paper. Wilson is the reigning MVP of the 2022 World Cup and the 2024 Olympics, and Plum has been one of the program's most reliable bench weapons at both events.Why A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum pulled outPlum's absence linked to a lower leg injury that has bothered her most of the WNBA season. She missed nearly six weeks earlier in the year, returned in August, then saw the injury flare up again after her trade from the Los Angeles Sparks to the Phoenix Mercury. The Mercury has since ruled her out for the rest of the WNBA season too.Wilson's situation is murkier. She has dealt with a back issue that popped up on the injury report twice in the past week, though she still played 30 minutes in her last game before the FIBA break.A source told ESPN she has not been fully healthy for a while and there was concern the World Cup's packed schedule would make things worse. Wilson had already hinted at this balancing act back in July. "I have given it some thought, not going to lie," she told The Dunker Spot, adding that she planned to let her body guide the decision as the moment got closer.Who will replace A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum?Team USA turned to two Washington Mystics teammates. Sonia Citron, who is averaging 16.8 points per game this season, steps in as a shooting guard rather than a natural point guard, which was Plum's primary role.Kiki Iriafen, one of the WNBA's better young power forwards, gives the frontcourt some of the depth it loses without Wilson. Iriafen already has international experience with this group, having played for the U.S. at the World Cup qualifying tournament in Puerto Rico back in March.What A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum's absence means for Team USAEven with a roster this deep, losing the best player in the world changes things. Wilson averaged a double-double in Paris, 18.7 points, 10.2 rebounds and 2.7 blocks a game, and closed the gold medal win over France with 21 points, 13 rebounds and four blocks. Plum's bench scoring helped hold off that same French team's late push. Replacing that kind of production is not simple.The schedule does not offer much room to adjust either. Team USA opens with three games in four days, and if it reaches the final, that becomes six games in ten. Kara Lawson is running her first major international tournament as head coach, though eight of the twelve players in Berlin were part of the Puerto Rico qualifying roster, which should help the group settle in faster than the circumstances suggest. Aliyah Boston, who has been playing through a leg issue of her own, is also worth watching as the minutes get redistributed.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

A 23-year-old man has been charged with murder following a fatal house fire.

Natalie McDonald, 34, died in the blaze in Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, in the early hours of Wednesday, along with her niece Valentina Foster, seven.

The man was charged with two counts of murder, two counts of grievous bodily harm with intent and two counts of attempted grievous bodily harm with intent, Cleveland Police say. He is scheduled to appear at Teesside Magistrates' Court later on Tuesday.

"This has been a truly tragic incident, and my thoughts remain with the families of all those involved," Senior Investigating Officer Katie Smith from Northumbria Police said.

"I would like to thank local residents for their support and patience during this complex investigation."

Anyone who may still have information, or has any concerns, can submit Information using the Major Incident Public Portal , she added.

Katie Nicolson, chief crown prosecutor for CPS North East, said: "Our prosecutors have worked closely with Cleveland Police to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court.

"We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial. It is vital that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information which could in anyway prejudice these proceedings."

articles.title: Major search for missing teen in Marloes Sands called off
articles.summary: The 15-year-old, from the Yorkshire area, was at Marloes Sands beach in Pembrokeshire.
articles.body:
A major sea search for a missing 15-year-old boy has been called off after two days, the Coastguard has said.

At about 15:30 BST on Sunday, HM Coastguard received a report that three people were experiencing difficulty in the water at Marloes Sands beach, Pembrokeshire.

Two managed to get out of the water, but the teenage boy, who was visiting the area on holiday from Yorkshire, was unaccounted for. The search was suspended at 19:30 BST on Monday.

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency told the BBC that there were currently no plans to resume the search.

In a statement on social media, Angle Lifeboat RNLI said its crew "worked tirelessly" for 22 hours at sea in a major, multi-agency search for the missing swimmer.

On Sunday, Broad Haven and Dale coastguard rescue teams were in attendance, alongside RNLI lifeboats from Angle, Tenby and St Davids and a pilot boat.

A coastguard helicopter and a HM Coastguard fixed wing aircraft were sent, along with the Welsh Ambulance Service.

The search was suspended at about 03:30 BST on Monday and started again later that morning, before being called off in the evening.

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency said, despite an extensive search, "sadly, no sign of the missing person was found".

Angle Lifeboat RNLI added its crew had "shown immense dedication over the past two days".

It thanked the Milford Haven Coastguard for "their fantastic coordination and support" in what they said has been a "lengthy and tiring incident".

"Our thoughts are with the swimmer's family and friends at this difficult time," it added.

articles.title: Will Burnham find PMQs as 'nail biting' and 'nerve wracking' as Blair did?
articles.summary: Curiously, the questions at lunchtime may well feel like a minor extension of what he faced on Tuesday, the BBC's political editor writes.
articles.body:
The weekly ritual that sits at the heart of Westminster's public image beckons, the half an hour or so of verbal jousting at Prime Minister's Questions (PMQs).

Prime ministerial memoirs tell the stories of how central a moment it is in the week of any occupant of 10 Downing Street.

Sir Tony Blair wrote that "PMQs was the most nerve wracking, discombobulating, nail biting, bowel moving, terror inspiring, courage draining experience in my prime ministerial life, without question".

Now, for the first time, it is Andy Burnham's turn to feel those nerves. And yet, curiously, the questions at lunchtime may well feel like a minor extension to the three and a half hours of questions he faced on Tuesday afternoon.

And this is because Parliament is playing catch-up: six weeks into the job, Burnham is encountering the moments that would typically arrive in the opening days, the routine moments of scrutiny in the House of Commons.

His arrival in office coincided with the departure of MPs from Westminster for the summer, and so the prime minister had a month or so that felt rather like a soft launch, heatwaves plentiful, Commons questions absent. Now plenty of them are coming, all at once.

I observed Andy Burnham's opening moments in the Commons as prime minister from the Press Gallery. He hovered by the Speaker's chair waiting his turn, flanked by Labour's Deputy Leader, Lucy Powell, who appeared to brush some fluff from the back of his jacket, and Louise Haigh, his first secretary of state.

Burnham promises more devolution and public control of essential services

Five takeaways from Burnham's Commons debut as PM

The dangers of politicians being 'too online' - or not online enough

The customary roar of approval from Labour MPs followed as he took his seat. Incidentally, MPs tend to manage this partisan and rather performative audible endorsement almost irrespective of the political weather their boss is encountering or indeed their role in creating it.

But having pondered whether to stick or twist a few months back, stick with Sir Keir Starmer or twist with another card, this was their first chance to see how he – Burnham – gets on in the role.

His opponents privately acknowledge his more upbeat demeanour, his sunnier disposition, is politically savvy, but they also spot laden political clouds to point at: prisons, overcrowded; defence, underfunded; social care, unreformed. A mere trio to zoom in on.

The new prime minister looked at ease making an argument and articulating his political creed. But beyond a few nuggets of news – he will attend the COP climate summit later this autumn, he blames Brexit for damaging the economy, he suggested, without detail, he would find the money to crank up defence spending – we did not learn much we did not already know.

His team hope this to be a pattern that becomes familiar – that ideas and plans are carefully dripped into the national conversation, taking shape and solidifying over time rather than appearing out of nowhere.

They are also keen to double down on the idea that Andy Burnham is seeking to be tonally and stylistically different in how he does the job. He has posted on social media:

"I want to be talking to you, the public, not just the House of Commons, so let's make it People's Major Questions rather than Prime Minister's Questions, so send me what you want to ask me and I'll answer them after the other PMQs."

It is an interesting idea that it will be interesting to keep an eye on – both today and over the coming months and years.

articles.body:
When the Detroit Lions released Terrion Arnold after his arrest, the team faced scrutiny for not doing enough to protect themself at the position. However, General Manager Brad Holmes made it clear that he feels good about the cornerback room, and they felt they had a good group whether Arnold was here or not.

"We like the guys we have in this room," said Holmes.

Detroit kept seven cornerbacks. Holmes feels that all of them serve a particular role.

Detroit Lions General Manager Defends Cornerback Room

Dave Birkett of the Detroit Free Press pushed back on Holmes, asking if he felt they could have done more this offseason.

"We did bring players in," replied Holmes firmly. "We did draft a corner; we did sign a corner in free agency; we did re-sign a corner."

Holmes went on to explain that they brought back D.J. Reed as a starter, and liked the idea of bringing back Rock Ya-Sin to start across from him.

"Rock played really good football for us last year; he had a really good camp this year," said Holmes on the player starting across from Reed.

Ya-Sin is entering his eighth year in the NFL , and he has 45 career starts. He started six games for the Lions last year. So, he has experience and is familiar with the defense.

Holmes added that beyond that, they felt comfortable with the depth to round out the room.

"Ennis (Rakestraw), we are just glad that his health has been better and that he has a chance to go out and compete," said Holmes. "He has gotten better throughout the camp; he has a lot of ability…We liked being able to bring Roger McCreary in…Then us being able to draft Keith Abney; he's been a quick study."

Holmes mentioned five cornerbacks, all with notable roles on the depth chart. Then, he added that sixth cornerback Khalil Dorsey is in the mix due to special teams.

"You still got Dors, who I think has been one of the better gunners in the league," Holmes mentioned. "So overall I think we have a group there."

He made it clear that adding a cornerback was not much of a consideration for the team, even after the Arnold release.

Lions Enter 2026 With Questions in the Secondary

As things stand, four of the five starters from last year will be different. Rock Ya-Sin will be starting across from Reed. Meanwhile, either Abney or McCreary will be working in the slot. Both would be new starters.

At safety, both Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph are starting the year on the PUP . So, the team will be starting Avonte Maddox and Chuck Clark at safety.

Maddox was with the team last year but served in a depth role. Clark is a free agent addition from the Pittsburgh Steelers .

With so much change and so many questions, it is easy to see why Holmes would be questioned. However, he made it clear they are happy with how things look entering the year.
